newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Opposition returns to streets after melee.
newsitem.headline: Opposition returns to streets after melee.

text.p: Undaunted by police beatings, opponents of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic took to Belgrade streets in protest again on Wednesday, demanding recognition of election results.
Belgrade's emergency medical centre treated 58 people for injuries on Tuesday after surging pro- and anti-Milosevic crowds clashed in the capital and police waded in to separate the factions.
Five were hospitalised, including one man who remained in critical condition after being shot in the head during the disturbances by a Socialist party (SPS) supporter.

More than a month of street protests against Milosevic and his ruling SPS party had gone virtually without violence until Tuesday when the SPS arranged to bus supporters into Belgrade for a rally at the same time and place as the opposition.
Vuk Draskovic, leader of the opposition Serbian Renewal Movement, said Tuesday's events let the genie of violence out of the bottle and marked "the beginning of civil war in Belgrade".
But Wednesday's protests began without trouble and with no sign of the previous day's massive police presence.
In what has become a ritual with carnival-like overtones, student protestors began assembling at noon for their own seperate march through city streets.

Snow, bitter temperatures, icy streets and the memory of Tuesday's running battles did little to dampen the students' enthusiasm although their numbers were down substantially from the previous day when about 40,000 marched.

Blowing whistles and horns and chanting anti-Milosevic slogans, they snaked through the centre of the city, drawing waves and cheers of support from many onlookers in office and residential blocks along the way.
The main opposition march was scheduled for mid-afternoon on the 36th straight day of demonstrations in the capital.
The protests were triggered after SPS-controlled committees overturned November 17 opposition victories in municipal elections in a number of cities and towns.

Washington and Paris warned on Tuesday they held Milosevic responsible for Belgrade's street violence. German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel warned any further violence would damage Serbia's efforts to reintegrate with Europe.

Western governments which spent much of the last year praising Slobodan Milosevic as a responsible world leader for his work in support of the Bosnian peace agreement are now distancing themselves from Europe's last communist dictator.

A fact-finding mission by the transatlantic Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) is expected within the week to deliver its view of the November 17 elections and of the tense political situation inside Serbia.
But Milosevic uses American and European criticism to his advantage among SPS supporters who believe their nation is a constant victim of western conspiracies.
Still firmly in control of all institutions of government, including state television, the army and police, Milosevic shows no sign of surrendering power voluntarily.

Diplomats say Russia would probably block any effort by the U.N. Security Council to pressure Milosevic by reimposing economic sanctions on Serbia, which were lifted earlier this year in the wake of the Bosnia peace deal.
